title: Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner
subject: Section 174 Treatment of Equipment Modification Expenditures
summary: Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 52 T.C. 682 (1969), aff'd, 429 F.2d 1 (10th Cir. 1970), is a foundational U.S. federal tax case for businesses claiming R&D deductions and credits. It holds that taxpayers must prove expenditures are experimental under IRC § 174 and segregate them from capital improvements, or the costs must be capitalized.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

In the jurisprudence governing United States federal research and development (R&D) tax incentives, Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 52 T.C. 682 (1969), aff'd, 429 F.2d 1 (10th Cir. 1970), stands as a foundational precedent delineating the boundary between currently deductible research or experimental expenditures under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 174 and nondeductible capital expenditures under IRC § 263. Handed down by Judge Dawson of the United States Tax Court and subsequently affirmed by Circuit Judge Seth of the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, the decision addressed an income tax deficiency of $145,183.25 determined by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue for the taxpayer's taxable year ended January 3, 1965 (referred to by the court as the taxable year 1964) under the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. Although adjudicated prior to the enactment of the incremental research tax credit in 1981—originally codified as IRC § 44F by the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, redesignated as IRC § 30 by the Deficit Reduction Act of 1984, redesignated as IRC § 41 by the Tax Reform Act of 1986, and made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015—Coors Porcelain remains a primary authority cited by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and federal courts to enforce the threshold requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) that qualified research expenditures must first be eligible for treatment as expenses under IRC § 174.
Factual Genesis and the Taxpayer's Claims

The petitioner, Coors Porcelain Company, headquartered in Golden, Colorado (and subsequently renamed Coors Ceramics and later CoorsTek), operated as a leading United States industrial manufacturer of chemical and scientific porcelain labware, high-purity alumina, and advanced technical ceramics. Having established its formal research and development group in the 1940s, the company expanded its specialized technical staff from two engineers in 1946 to 65 engineers across ceramics, chemistry, metallurgy, mineralogy, and physics by 1962 to support complex industrial and defense manufacturing applications. After the parties' concessions, four issues remained for decision by the Tax Court: an extraordinary obsolescence loss deduction on the Fuel Elements Building, the useful life of that building for depreciation purposes, the treatment of amounts spent on certain items of equipment, and deductions for depreciation and a loss on scrapped equipment relating to an erroneously duplicated electrical substation; this report focuses on the two claims that intersected most directly with the taxpayer's manufacturing equipment and specialized research and production facilities.

The first disputed claim involved an expenditure of $5,655.80 incurred during the 1964 taxable year to modify and convert the feeding device of the taxpayer's besly grinder (a double-disk ceramic grinder) from an oscillatory feed to a rotary feed-through motion so that the machine would function in a different and improved manner (the same issue also covered $2,292.25 spent to develop a position loader and $477.24 spent to develop an X-Y positioner). Coors Porcelain deducted this amount as a business expense on its 1964 federal income tax return and, before the Tax Court, contended that the costs were deductible either as expenses for repairs or as experimental expenditures, the latter argument being evaluated by the court under IRC § 174(a).

The second disputed claim involved a substantial deduction for extraordinary obsolescence and sudden loss of useful value on a specialized structure known as the Fuel Elements Building. In 1960, Coors Porcelain obtained a contract from the United States Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) to produce ceramic nuclear fuel elements to be used in supersonic low-altitude flying reactor missiles (a program historically associated with Project Pluto). Because the manufacture of the fuel elements was extremely hazardous owing to the dangers of nuclear chain reactions and contamination, the company in 1961 specifically constructed the Fuel Elements Building at its own cost of $464,072.82, designed and built according to AEC specifications and supervision. At some time in 1964, the AEC canceled the contract and license authorizing Coors Porcelain to produce the ceramic nuclear fuel elements (a cancellation the Tenth Circuit attributed to a treaty entered into between the United States and Russia), and because the fuel elements could be produced only pursuant to Government authority, the cancellation caused Coors Porcelain to terminate its production of them completely. On its 1964 return, in addition to taking a deduction for ordinary depreciation of $38,115.74 (computed using a 20-year useful life), the taxpayer claimed a $223,225.42 extraordinary obsolescence loss deduction on the building, which the Tax Court analyzed under IRC § 165(a) and Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-8 (on appeal the taxpayer characterized it as an obsolescence allowance under IRC § 167), asserting that the cancellation of the AEC contract abruptly terminated the economic usefulness of the building.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon examination of the 1964 return, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed both deductions and issued a statutory notice of deficiency. Addressing the $5,655.80 equipment modification expenditure (together with the position loader and X-Y positioner costs), the Commissioner determined that the amounts were nondeductible capital expenditures. Before the Tax Court, the government asserted that the expenditures resulted in adapting the grinder to a new and different use, or in a permanent improvement, the cost of which constitutes a capital expenditure under IRC § 263(a) recoverable through depreciation deductions over the asset's useful life. The opinion does not recite a separate argument by the Commissioner responding to the taxpayer's alternative experimental-expenditure contention; it was the Tax Court itself that found the record contained no evidence that the expenditures were experimental expenditures within the meaning of IRC § 174(a), no evidence permitting possibly experimental costs to be segregated from excluded material, labor, construction, and installation costs, and no evidence that the taxpayer had adopted the IRC § 174(a) method in its first eligible year or obtained the Commissioner's consent.

With respect to the Fuel Elements Building, the Commissioner disallowed the $223,225.42 extraordinary obsolescence loss deduction in full on the ground that the taxpayer failed to establish entitlement to it, and determined that the building's useful life for computing ordinary depreciation was 40 years rather than the 20 years claimed. The Commissioner argued that the continued use of the building, both actual and contemplated, precluded any obsolescence deduction, and that a mere diminution in value while assets are still used is not a proper basis for an obsolescence deduction; the Tax Court, applying Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-8, required proof that the building's usefulness suddenly terminated in the taxable year and that the building was permanently withdrawn from use in the taxpayer's trade or business. Because Coors Porcelain moved its research and spectrochemical laboratory operations into the Fuel Elements Building after the AEC contract termination and continued that use through the January 1969 trial, while its officers were still trying to find another, more suitable use for the structure, the Commissioner contended that no permanent retirement or extraordinary obsolescence had occurred in 1964.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute in Coors Porcelain was adjudicated under the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, implicating an interconnected framework of deduction, capitalization, and depreciation statutes that remain central to modern United States R&D tax controversies. Under IRC § 174(a)(1) of the 1954 Code, a taxpayer was authorized to treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year in connection with its trade or business as currently deductible expenses not chargeable to a capital account, provided the taxpayer validly adopted that method in its first eligible taxable year under IRC § 174(a)(2)(A) or obtained the consent of the Secretary under IRC § 174(a)(2)(B) and (a)(3). An alternative election under IRC § 174(b) allowed taxpayers to treat non-depreciable research expenditures as deferred expenses amortizable over a period of not less than 60 months. Crucially, however, IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1) expressly excluded from IRC § 174 treatment any expenditure for the acquisition or improvement of land, or for the acquisition or improvement of property to be used in connection with research or experimentation if that property is of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167, stipulating that only the periodic depreciation allowances attributable to the research use of such property may be treated as IRC § 174 expenditures.

Because Congress did not exhaustively define the phrase "research or experimental expenditures" in the text of IRC § 174, the governing regulatory standard is set forth in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), which defines the term as expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that represent "research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense". In later decisions applying this regulation, courts have given the terms "experimental" and "laboratory" their plain and ordinary meanings, requiring that the activity have a scientifically reasonable goal and involve genuine experimentation applying scientific principles in testing and analysis to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process (the uncertainty language was added to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) in 1994; in Coors Porcelain, the Tax Court did not undertake this analysis but simply cited Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2 for the general definition and found the record silent on experimentation).

Operating alongside IRC § 174 are the general business deduction and capitalization provisions of IRC § 162(a) and IRC § 263(a). While IRC § 162(a) allows a current deduction for ordinary and necessary business expenses, including incidental repairs that keep property in an ordinarily efficient operating condition, IRC § 263(a) and Treas. Reg. § 1.263(a)-1(b) prohibit current deductions for permanent improvements or betterments made to increase the value of property, appreciably prolong its useful life, or adapt the property to a new or different use. For property that is capitalized, IRC § 167(a) provides a reasonable depreciation allowance for exhaustion, wear and tear, and normal obsolescence, whereas deductions for the sudden termination of usefulness, extraordinary obsolescence, or permanent retirement of a depreciable asset are governed by the loss provisions of IRC § 165(a) and the retirement and obsolescence rules of Treas. Reg. §§ 1.167(a)-8 and 1.167(a)-9.

In contemporary United States tax law, the statutory framework interpreted in Coors Porcelain serves as the mandatory legal threshold for the incremental research tax credit under IRC § 41. Under IRC § 41(a)(1) and § 41(b), a taxpayer may claim a tax credit based on qualified research expenses (QREs)—consisting of in-house research wages, supplies, certain computer leasing costs, and a statutory percentage of contract research expenses—paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business. Under IRC § 41(d)(1), an activity constitutes "qualified research" only if it satisfies a cumulative Four-Part Test: first, under the Section 174 Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), the expenditures connected with the research must be eligible for treatment as expenses under IRC § 174; second, under the Technological in Nature Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature; third, under the Business Component Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the application of that information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer; and fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and (d)(3), substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. As confirmed by the Tax Court in Norwest Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, 110 T.C. 454, 491 (1998), and reiterated by the IRS in Field Attorney Advice memoranda FAA 20131102F and FAA 20154501F, the requirement in IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) that expenditures "may be treated as expenses under section 174" requires the taxpayer to satisfy all substantive elements for deductibility/amortization under IRC § 174, making Coors Porcelain directly controlling in modern IRC § 41 controversies. Furthermore, even following the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA) amendments to IRC § 174 requiring capitalization and amortization of specified research or experimental expenditures for post-2021 years (and subsequent domestic R&D cost-recovery provisions under IRC § 174A), the substantive definition of research or experimental expenditures under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2 and the evidentiary standards of Coors Porcelain remain unaltered.
The Court's Final Holding

The United States Tax Court sustained the Commissioner's determinations on all disputed issues. Addressing the $5,655.80 besly grinder modification at 52 T.C. 696–698, Judge Dawson held that because the taxpayer did not mend or restore the grinder to a sound state but altered or improved it to function in a different manner, the costs were for a permanent improvement or betterment made to increase the value of the grinder and were therefore capital expenditures under IRC § 263(a) rather than deductible repair expenses. Crucially, the Tax Court held that Coors Porcelain had not established its right to treat the expenditures as deductible expenses under IRC § 174(a) for two reasons: first, aside from the taxpayer's naked allegation, there was no evidence that the expenditures constituted experimental expenditures within the meaning of IRC § 174(a) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2, and because the costs of component material, labor, and other elements of construction and installation are excluded by Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4), the absence of evidence made it impossible to segregate any possibly experimental costs; and second, there was no evidence that 1964 was the first year in which the taxpayer incurred research or experimental expenditures or that it obtained the Commissioner's consent under IRC § 174(a)(2)(B), so the expenditures had to be charged to capital account under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-1. The court likewise held that the $2,292.25 and $477.24 spent developing the position loader and X-Y positioner were capital expenditures, because both machines were placed in production use by the end of 1964 and were found unsatisfactory and replaced only in April 1965.

Regarding the Fuel Elements Building (52 T.C. at 688–695), the Tax Court affirmed the Commissioner's disallowance of the extraordinary obsolescence and retirement loss deduction. The court concluded that the appropriate statutory provision for a loss from extraordinary obsolescence of depreciable property occurring within one year is IRC § 165(a), with Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-8 supplying the governing rules, and that Coors Porcelain failed to prove either that the building's usefulness suddenly terminated in 1964 or that the building was permanently withdrawn from use, as evidenced by the company's continued and consistent use of the facility for its research and spectrochemical laboratory operations until the 1969 trial and its officers' ongoing efforts to find another use for the building; the court also sustained the Commissioner's 40-year (rather than 20-year) useful life for the building and disallowed the $829.26 depreciation and $34,409.13 scrapped-equipment deductions relating to the erroneously duplicated substation. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's judgment in full in Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 429 F.2d 1 (10th Cir. 1970), holding that the record showed no permanent withdrawal of the Fuel Elements Building, or any part of it, from use in the taxpayer's trade or business and that the Tax Court's 40-year useful-life finding was supported by substantial evidence, while expressly declining to decide whether IRC § 165 or IRC § 167 governed the obsolescence claim (the Tenth Circuit's opinion addressed only the obsolescence and useful-life issues).
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A comprehensive legal and technical evaluation of Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 52 T.C. at 688–698, alongside subsequent judicial and IRS administrative rulings applying the decision, reveals five distinct legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies that resulted in the disqualification of the taxpayer's claims.
1. Failure to Prove Technological Uncertainty and Activity in the Experimental or Laboratory Sense

The foundational substantive defect in Coors Porcelain was the taxpayer's failure to carry its affirmative burden of proof establishing that the $5,655.80 machinery modification expenditure satisfied the definition of "research or experimental expenditures" under IRC § 174 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1). In federal tax litigation, deductions and credits are matters of legislative grace, and as the IRS and courts consistently cite Coors Porcelain to enforce, the taxpayer bears the strict burden of establishing the right to treat expenditures as qualifying R&D expenses under IRC § 174.

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), as amended in 1994 (long after Coors Porcelain was decided), expenditures qualify as research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense" only when they are incurred for activities intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or manufacturing process. Uncertainty exists for purposes of IRC § 174 only if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or process, or the appropriate design of that product or process. Furthermore, federal tax jurisprudence requires that the goal of the research be scientifically reasonable and incorporate an authentic element of experimentation that applies scientific principles in testing and analysis.

In Coors Porcelain, the taxpayer demonstrated only that it had spent $5,655.80 to convert the feeding device of its besly grinder from an oscillatory feed to a rotary feed-through motion. Aside from the taxpayer's naked allegation that the expenditures were for experimentation, the record was silent on whether they constituted experimental expenditures; the Tax Court did not frame its analysis in terms of technological uncertainty, which was not then part of the regulatory definition. The only authority the taxpayer cited, Kent Machine Co. v. Commissioner, 168 F.2d 68 (6th Cir. 1948), was found distinguishable on its facts, and the record contained no evidence describing any experimental activity at all. Absent any evidence that the expenditures were experimental expenditures within the meaning of IRC § 174(a) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2, the Tax Court rejected the IRC § 174 characterization. In contemporary IRC § 41 examinations, this exact failure simultaneously defeats the Section 174 Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and the Process of Experimentation Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), as routine engineering modifications and production retooling do not constitute a scientific process of experimentation.
2. The Capital Improvement Bar and Depreciable Property Exclusion

The second fatal deficiency in Coors Porcelain stemmed from the statutory prohibition against deducting capital equipment improvements and depreciable property acquisitions as current repairs or R&D expenses under IRC § 162(a), IRC § 263(a), and IRC § 174(c). At 52 T.C. 697, the Tax Court found that the $5,655.80 expenditure physically altered the equipment and changed its function. Under IRC § 263(a) and Treas. Reg. § 1.263(a)-1(b), while incidental repairs that merely maintain an asset in an ordinarily efficient operating condition are deductible under IRC § 162(a), expenditures that materially add to the value of property, appreciably prolong its useful life, or adapt the property to a new or different use must be capitalized. Because the taxpayer did not mend or restore the grinder to a sound state but altered or improved it to function in a different manner, the Tax Court agreed with the Commissioner and held that the expenditures were for a permanent improvement or betterment made to increase the value of the grinder, requiring capitalization under IRC § 263(a); the court also noted that IRC § 263(a)(1)(B) excepts research and experimental expenditures deductible under IRC § 174, an exception the taxpayer failed to establish.

Equally significant was the depreciable property rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4), which the Tax Court invoked to hold that the costs of the component material of the modification, the cost of labor, and other elements involved in its construction and installation are specifically excluded from experimental expenditures (the court did not separately cite IRC § 174(c), which embodies the same depreciable property exclusion). Under IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1)–(2), expenditures for the acquisition, construction, or improvement of property of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167 are expressly excluded from IRC § 174 deductibility, even if the machine or facility is used exclusively in research or experimentation. Under current regulations, the costs of producing a "pilot model" (defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), added in 2014, as any representation or model of a product produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement) may qualify under IRC § 174 even if the pilot model is later used in the trade or business or sold; otherwise, the component material, labor, and installation costs of modifying a depreciable machine must be capitalized into a fixed-asset account. Only the annual depreciation allowances under IRC § 167 attributable to the period and percentage of time the machine is actually used in qualifying research activities may be treated as IRC § 174 expenditures. Furthermore, under the modern research tax credit of IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b), property of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation is strictly excluded from qualifying as supply QREs, and depreciation allowances themselves are entirely ineligible for the IRC § 41 credit. By deducting the full cost of modifying a depreciable production machine as a current business expense and then arguing in the alternative for IRC § 174 treatment without evidence segregating any experimental costs, Coors Porcelain ran afoul of both IRC § 263(a) and the depreciable property rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4).
3. Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation and Failure to Segregate Costs

The third critical failure articulated by the Tax Court at 52 T.C. 697–698 was the taxpayer's inability to segregate potentially qualifying experimental costs from non-qualifying capital improvement expenses. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4) (the provision cited by the Tax Court), when research or experimental activities are conducted in connection with the construction, manufacture, or modification of depreciable property, the taxpayer may claim IRC § 174 treatment only for the discrete, preliminary experimental engineering and testing costs incurred to resolve technological uncertainty regarding the design of the asset, whereas all costs of physically constructing, fabricating, or installing the depreciable property itself must be capitalized.

In Coors Porcelain, the taxpayer presented a single aggregated expenditure of $5,655.80 without introducing any evidence (such as cost records, work orders, or labor and material breakdowns) separating possibly experimental costs from the component material, labor, construction, and installation costs of the grinder modification, and although it asserted that part of the amount was for replacing worn-out belts and sheaves, it provided no data on their cost. As the Tax Court emphasized, the complete absence of granular evidence prevented the court from separating any qualifying experimental activity from general capital improvements and non-qualifying expenses. Because the absence of evidence made segregation impossible, the court held that the entire $5,655.80 had to be charged to capital account under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-1, sustaining the disallowance of the deduction.

This strict anti-commingling holding in Coors Porcelain forms the backbone of modern IRS substantiation enforcement under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d). In contemporary IRC § 41 litigation—including Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84—federal courts consistently reject "all-or-nothing" project cost aggregations and decline to apply the Cohan estimation doctrine where taxpayers fail to maintain contemporaneous records establishing a nexus between specific wages or supplies and qualified experimental activities. Similarly, in FAA 20131102F and FAA 20154501F, the IRS Office of Chief Counsel relied directly on Coors Porcelain, 52 T.C. at 697–698, to disallow Voluntary Separation Program (VSP) severance payments and unsubstantiated executive compensation from QREs because the taxpayers failed to establish through contemporaneous evidence that the specific costs met every element of IRC § 174.
4. Procedural Failure to Prove Valid Adoption or Election of the Section 174 Method

In addition to the substantive and evidentiary defects, the Tax Court held at 52 T.C. 697–698 that Coors Porcelain failed to prove that it had properly adopted or elected the IRC § 174 method for the disputed expenditures. Under IRC § 174(a)(2) of the 1954 Code and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-3, a taxpayer was permitted to adopt the current-expense method without the consent of the Commissioner only in the first taxable year in which it paid or incurred research or experimental expenditures, and had to do so by claiming the deduction openly on its timely filed income tax return for that first year. Once a taxpayer established an accounting practice of capitalizing equipment modification costs or deducting them solely under an IRC § 162 repair theory, reclassifying those expenditures to IRC § 174 constituted a change in method of accounting requiring the prior consent of the Commissioner under IRC § 174(a)(3) and IRC § 446(e).

Because Coors Porcelain, which had deducted the $5,655.80 as a business expense on its return, argued before the Tax Court that the amount was alternatively deductible as an experimental expenditure without introducing any evidence that 1964 was the first taxable year in which it incurred research or experimental expenditures or that it had obtained the Commissioner's consent under IRC § 174(a)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-3(b)(2), the Tax Court held that the expenditures did not qualify for treatment as expenses under IRC § 174(a). For modern United States tax practitioners, this procedural requirement remains vital when navigating accounting method changes between IRC § 263(a) fixed-asset capitalization, IRC § 174 capitalization and amortization, and IRC § 174A domestic R&D cost recovery via Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method).
5. Government Contract Cancellation, Dual-Use Laboratory Facilities, and the Obsolescence and Funded Research Traps

The Tax Court's and Tenth Circuit's holdings regarding the Fuel Elements Building (52 T.C. at 688–695, aff'd, 429 F.2d 1) expose profound legal and contractual pitfalls for taxpayers performing specialized defense or commercial R&D contracts. Coors Porcelain asserted that because it constructed the Fuel Elements Building specifically to produce ceramic nuclear fuel elements under its 1960 AEC contract, the government's cancellation of the contract in 1964 (which the Tenth Circuit attributed to a treaty entered into between the United States and Russia) abruptly ended the building's useful life, justifying an extraordinary obsolescence or abandonment loss deduction under IRC § 167(a) or IRC § 165(a).

Both courts rejected this contention because the objective post-cancellation conduct of the taxpayer contradicted any claim of permanent retirement or total worthlessness. Specifically, after halting production of the nuclear fuel elements in 1964, Coors Porcelain moved its research and spectrochemical laboratory operations into the Fuel Elements Building and continued that use until the January 1969 trial, some five years later, while its officers testified that they were still trying to find another, more suitable use for the building and that no decision had been made. Under IRC § 165(a) and Treas. Reg. §§ 1.167(a)-8 and 1.167(a)-9, a taxpayer cannot claim a retirement or extraordinary obsolescence loss merely because a single government contract is cancelled or an asset suffers a diminution in economic value while it remains in use; rather, under the Tax Court's reading of Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-8, the taxpayer must show both that the asset's usefulness suddenly terminated in the taxable year and that the asset was permanently withdrawn from use in the trade or business. The Tax Court further noted that even if certain specialized features of the building (such as the waste disposal system, the vault, the high open bay, and some of the specialized chemical piping) became obsolete in 1964, no deduction could be allowed for them because the taxpayer made no effort to segregate and identify their undepreciated cost.

Furthermore, the intersection of the AEC defense contract and the continued laboratory use of the Fuel Elements Building in Coors Porcelain would implicate, under today's law (the court itself never addressed the issue, as the research credit was not enacted until 1981), a critical modern disqualification trigger under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H): the funded research exclusion. Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), qualified research excludes any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. In evaluating defense and commercial contracts under this exclusion, United States courts examine two mandatory contractual prongs: first, whether the researcher's right to payment is contingent upon the technical success of the research such that the researcher bears the financial risk of failure (Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995); Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015); Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024)); and second, whether the researcher retains "substantial rights" in the resulting research without having to pay for their use (Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000); Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Dkt. No. 405-17 (Dec. 6, 2019) (order granting summary judgment); Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1). When a defense contractor conducts research inside a facility built for a federal agency contract and subsequently transitions that facility to internal laboratory use upon contract termination, failing to structure the underlying contracts to preserve financial risk and substantial IP rights—and failing to segregate government-reimbursed contract closeout costs from self-funded Independent Research and Development (IR&D)—will result in the complete disallowance of IRC § 41 research credits.
Comparative Summary Table

The following Markdown table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement addressed in Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner (alongside its contemporary integration into IRC § 174 and IRC § 41) against the taxpayer's specific failure and the governing judicial standard of proof established by the Tax Court and the Tenth Circuit.

Court's Governing Standard of Proof & Holding

cells: Eligibility as R&D in the Experimental or Laboratory Sense (IRC § 174(a); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1); modern gateway to IRC § 41(d)(1)(A))

Coors Porcelain deducted $5,655.80 in besly grinder modification costs as a business expense and argued alternatively that they were experimental expenditures under IRC § 174, but offered nothing beyond a naked allegation; the record was silent on whether the expenditures were experimental.

Affirmative Proof of Experimental Activity: The taxpayer bears the burden of establishing clear entitlement to IRC § 174 treatment. The taxpayer must present evidence that the expenditures constitute experimental expenditures within the meaning of IRC § 174(a) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2; a naked allegation of experimentation is insufficient (the uncertainty-based definition now in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) was added in 1994).
Distinction Between Deductible Repairs/R&D and Capital Improvements (IRC § 162(a); IRC § 263(a); Treas. Reg. § 1.263(a)-1(b))

The taxpayer sought an immediate deduction for converting its besly grinder's feeding device from an oscillatory to a rotary feed-through motion so that the machine would function in a different and improved manner.

Functional Alteration Requires Capitalization: Where expenditures do not mend or restore a machine to a sound state but alter or improve it to function in a different manner, they are for a permanent improvement or betterment made to increase its value and must be capitalized under IRC § 263(a) rather than deducted currently as repairs.
Exclusion of Depreciable Property Improvements from Current R&D Expensing (IRC § 174(c); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1)–(2); IRC § 41(b)(2)(C))

The taxpayer sought to deduct the full cost of modifying depreciable production machinery, including component material, labor, and installation costs, without evidence isolating any experimental portion.

Capitalization of Depreciable Assets Used in R&D: The Tax Court held that the costs of component material, labor, and other elements involved in constructing and installing the modification are specifically excluded from experimental expenditures by Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4); consistent with IRC § 174(c), only depreciation allowances attributable to research use may be treated as IRC § 174 expenditures (and depreciation is wholly excluded from IRC § 41 QREs).
Cost Segregation & Contemporaneous Substantiation of R&D vs. Capital Costs (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3)–(4); IRC § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d))

The taxpayer presented a lump-sum expenditure of $5,655.80 without any evidence segregating possibly experimental costs from excluded construction and installation costs, and offered no cost data even for the worn-out belts and sheaves it said were replaced.

Granular Bifurcation Mandate: The absence of specific, contemporaneous evidence prevents the court from separating potentially qualifying experimental costs from general capital improvements. Without an evidentiary basis for segregation, the entire expenditure must be charged to capital account under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-1.
Procedural Adoption or Election of the IRC § 174 Accounting Method (IRC § 174(a)(2)–(3); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-3; IRC § 446(e))

Coors Porcelain raised IRC § 174 as an alternative litigation theory without introducing proof in the record that it had properly adopted the IRC § 174 method in its first eligible year or obtained the Commissioner's consent to change its method for equipment costs.

Strict Procedural Compliance: A taxpayer cannot claim IRC § 174 treatment unless it affirmatively proves on the record that it timely adopted the method in accordance with Treasury Regulations or secured formal IRS consent under IRC § 174 and IRC § 446(e) to change its accounting treatment.
Extraordinary Obsolescence, Retirement Loss, and Useful Life of R&D/Contract Facilities (IRC § 165(a); IRC § 167(a); Treas. Reg. §§ 1.167(a)-8 & -9)

Following the 1964 cancellation of the AEC nuclear fuel elements contract, Coors Porcelain claimed a $223,225.42 extraordinary obsolescence loss deduction on the Fuel Elements Building while continuing to use it for its research and spectrochemical laboratory operations through the 1969 trial and still trying to find another use for it.

Proof of Permanent Abandonment and Worthlessness: A loss from extraordinary obsolescence under IRC § 165(a) and Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-8 requires proof that the asset's usefulness suddenly terminated in the taxable year and that the asset was permanently withdrawn from use. Continued laboratory use and management's search for alternative applications defeat any claim of abandonment or extraordinary obsolescence.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how United States taxpayers and R&D tax advisors can proactively structure engineering operations to overcome the exact legal, contractual, accounting, and evidentiary pitfalls identified in Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, the following two detailed industry case studies provide step-by-step remedial blueprints.
Case Study 1: Advanced Technical Ceramics Manufacturer — Overcoming Equipment Modification, Capital Retooling, and Cost Segregation Pitfalls
Industry Scenario and Project Background

AluminaTech Ceramics Corp. ("AluminaTech"), a Delaware C-corporation manufacturing advanced technical ceramics in Golden, Colorado, initiates "Project HyperSinter" during the current taxable year. AluminaTech seeks to develop a novel, ultra-pure (99.995%) silicon carbide (SiC) and aluminum nitride (AlN) composite wafer susceptor capable of withstanding extreme plasma erosion inside next-generation Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) semiconductor lithography chambers. To achieve the required zero-porosity microstructure, AluminaTech engineers hypothesize that an existing continuous-feed tunnel kiln and cold isostatic press (CIP) line must be fundamentally re-engineered to introduce a multi-zone, microwave-assisted reactive sintering atmosphere at under dynamic argon-nitrogen partial pressure. Prior to the project, fundamental technological uncertainty exists because available scientific and engineering data do not establish whether microwave coupling into the existing kiln refractory geometry will induce catastrophic thermal-runaway arcing, nor do they establish the exact binder-burnout and pressure-ramp algorithms needed to prevent micro-fissures across 450mm ceramic blanks.

In its unguided operational state, AluminaTech's finance department authorizes a single Capital Expenditure Request (CER #409) titled "Kiln #3 & CIP Line Reconstruction for EUV Susceptor Production" with a lump-sum budget of $1,850,000. Under CER #409, internal ceramic engineers, shop machinists, and an outside industrial kiln contractor spend nine months designing experimental microwave waveguides, fabricating three prototype refractory muffles (two of which fracture and are scrapped during high-temperature trials), executing 42 destructive sintering test batches, and ultimately installing permanent microwave magnetron banks and upgraded PLC controls onto Kiln #3, permanently changing the kiln's function from conventional oxide firing to microwave-assisted non-oxide sintering. At year-end, AluminaTech attempts to treat the entire $1,850,000 accumulated in CER #409 as IRC § 174 research expenditures and claims the associated internal labor, prototype materials, and contractor invoices as QREs under IRC § 41.
Identification of the Coors Porcelain Legal Pitfalls

Under an IRS examination, AluminaTech's tax position faces complete disqualification under Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 52 T.C. at 697–698. First, modifying Kiln #3 and the CIP line physically altered existing depreciable machinery and permanently changed its function, rendering the hardware conversion a capital improvement under IRC § 263(a) that is expressly excluded from IRC § 174 treatment by IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1). Second, by accumulating all preliminary experimental engineering, destructive trial runs, scrapped prototype muffles, and permanent magnetron hardware inside a single capital work order (CER #409), AluminaTech replicated Coors Porcelain's fatal evidentiary failure: the absence of granular cost segregation prevents the IRS or the Tax Court from separating qualifying experimental costs from non-qualifying capital improvements under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3)–(4). Third, labeling the project a "Kiln Reconstruction" obscures the underlying experimental ceramic science, while attempting to reclassify costs from a capital work order to IRC § 174 on the tax return without proper accounting method alignment violates the procedural mandates of IRC § 174 and IRC § 446(e).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Restructure Project Governance and Bifurcate Accounting Work Orders

Before incurring any project costs, AluminaTech's tax and engineering leadership must abolish the monolithic CER #409 work order and establish a three-tier General Ledger (GL) and Work Order architecture that strictly segregates experimental activities from capital improvements in compliance with Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3) and (b)(4). Specifically, AluminaTech must open Work Order R&D-409A (Experimental Process & Material Formulation) as an R&D expense sub-account dedicated exclusively to capturing internal engineering wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and raw ceramic powder and gas consumables under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) incurred in formulating the SiC-AlN slurry, modeling electromagnetic thermal gradients, and executing the 42 destructive sintering test runs to eliminate process uncertainty. Concurrently, AluminaTech must open Work Order R&D-409B (Expendable Pilot Models & Experimental Test Apparatus) under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) to capture the design, fabrication, and destructive testing of the temporary microwave waveguide test rigs and prototype refractory muffles built solely to evaluate design alternatives and destroyed prior to commercial readiness. Finally, AluminaTech must isolate all permanent machine construction in Work Order CAP-409C (Capital Asset Improvement & Production Retooling), an IRC § 263(a) fixed-asset account that captures the acquisition, physical installation, and mechanical integration of the permanent magnetron hardware, electrical switchgear, and structural modifications to Kiln #3 once the appropriate engineering design is validated.
Step 2: Establish Contemporaneous Technical Documentation of Uncertainty and Experimentation

To satisfy the Coors Porcelain requirement that the taxpayer prove with evidence that its expenditures are experimental expenditures, that is, R&D in the "experimental or laboratory sense" (52 T.C. at 697–698; Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)), AluminaTech must implement a formal stage-gate technical documentation protocol. Prior to modifying any hardware, the Principal Ceramic Engineer must execute a dated Technical Uncertainty Charter documenting why existing firing curves and conventional kiln configurations cannot achieve less than porosity in 450mm SiC-AlN susceptors without dielectric breakdown, thereby establishing objective capability, method, and design uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1). For each of the 42 trial runs conducted under Work Order R&D-409A, engineers must maintain contemporaneous Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN) records detailing the specific scientific hypothesis tested (such as varying 2.45 GHz versus 5.8 GHz microwave pulse modulation during the to thermal ramp), quantitative test results (including scanning electron microscopy porosity measurements and ultrasonic crack detection), and the iterative engineering modifications leading to the next trial. Crucially, the exact date on which Trial Run #42 confirms the optimal microwave waveguide geometry and firing algorithm must be memorialized via a signed Certificate of Experimental Validation, establishing a bright-line cut-off gate after which all subsequent labor and hardware work on Kiln #3 is routed strictly to Work Order CAP-409C as a capital improvement under IRC § 263(a).
Step 3: Restructure Third-Party Vendor and Equipment Integrator Contracts

In the original scenario, AluminaTech engaged an outside kiln contractor under a single lump-sum contract to reconstruct Kiln #3, causing the entire contractor fee to be treated as a capitalized cost of improving depreciable property under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(2). To remediate this contractual defect, AluminaTech must execute two separate legal instruments with the vendor prior to the performance of services: first, a Research and Experimental Engineering Services Agreement limited strictly to finite-element electromagnetic simulation and experimental waveguide testing (mapped to Work Order R&D-409A); and second, a separate Capital Equipment Fabrication and Installation Purchase Order for the permanent hardware build (mapped to Work Order CAP-409C). To ensure the engineering services agreement qualifies as contract research under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), the contract must explicitly stipulate that the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the research, that the experimental engineering is performed on behalf of AluminaTech, that AluminaTech retains exclusive ownership and substantial rights to all resulting designs and technical data, and that AluminaTech bears the financial risk of paying for the vendor's engineering hours regardless of whether the experimental waveguide design succeeds.
Step 4: Implement Precision Cost Tracking and Section 174 and Section 41 Tax Compliance

To complete the remediation, AluminaTech must enforce daily project timekeeping in which internal engineers and machinists log hours against specific task codes tied to Work Orders R&D-409A, R&D-409B, and CAP-409C, ensuring that only W-2 wages attributable to qualified experimental testing under R&D-409A and R&D-409B are included in IRC § 41(b)(2)(A) wage QREs, while shop-floor labor spent installing permanent capital hardware under CAP-409C is excluded. For the two prototype refractory muffles under R&D-409B that cracked during thermal testing, AluminaTech must preserve Contemporaneous Scrap Certificates and photographic evidence proving physical destruction during testing so those costs qualify as non-depreciable pilot models and supply QREs under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) and IRC § 41(b)(2)(C). Conversely, the permanent hardware and installation costs in CAP-409C must be capitalized under IRC § 263(a) and depreciated under IRC § 167 and § 168; to the extent Kiln #3 is subsequently used 20% of the year for experimental trials, 20% of its annual depreciation allowance may be treated as an IRC § 174(c) expenditure under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1), while being strictly excluded from the IRC § 41 credit computation. Finally, AluminaTech must confirm that its federal tax returns reflect a validly adopted IRC § 174 / § 174A accounting method (filing Form 3115 under IRC § 446(e) if changing the treatment of any previously misclassified accounts), thereby neutralizing the procedural bar identified in Coors Porcelain, 52 T.C. at 697–698.

body.text: Case Study 2: Aerospace and Defense Propulsion Contractor — Overcoming Contract Termination, Funded Research, and Dual-Use Facility Obsolescence Pitfalls
Industry Scenario and Project Background

VectraMat Defense Systems, Inc. ("VectraMat"), a United States aerospace and defense contractor, is awarded a multi-year prime contract by a federal defense agency in 2023 to develop and manufacture ultra-high-temperature ceramic matrix composite (CMC) scramjet combustion liners for a hypersonic missile program. To perform the contract, VectraMat constructs "Building 7," a $12,000,000 specialized Chemical Vapor Infiltration (CVI) and Plasma-Arc Wind Tunnel Facility on its corporate campus. In mid-2026, following a shift in federal strategic defense posture and international arms-control realignments, the federal government issues a formal Termination for Convenience cancelling the hypersonic missile contract. At the time of termination, Building 7 has an unrecovered adjusted tax basis of $9,200,000.

Following the contract cancellation, VectraMat ceases manufacturing the missile combustion liners. However, VectraMat retains 18 aerospace materials scientists inside Building 7's plasma-arc testing bay to conduct internal Independent Research and Development (IR&D) on reusable commercial orbital reentry thermal protection tiles, while corporate executives actively market Building 7's CVI reactor capacity to commercial satellite propulsion manufacturers. On its 2026 federal income tax return, VectraMat attempts to claim an immediate $9,200,000 extraordinary obsolescence and abandonment loss deduction on Building 7 under IRC § 165(a) and IRC § 167(a), asserting that the cancellation of the federal missile contract destroyed the economic usefulness of the facility. Simultaneously, VectraMat claims $3,400,000 in IRC § 41 QREs encompassing both the engineering wages and materials incurred on the federal hypersonic contract prior to termination (which was structured as a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee contract with standard government data rights) and the post-termination IR&D conducted inside Building 7.
Identification of the Coors Porcelain Legal Pitfalls

VectraMat's tax posture replicates the exact factual and legal vulnerabilities of the AEC Project Pluto contract and Fuel Elements Building in Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 52 T.C. at 688–695, aff'd, 429 F.2d 1 (10th Cir. 1970), compounded by modern IRC § 41 funded-research exclusions. First, under the square holding of Coors Porcelain, the cancellation of a specialized federal defense contract does not entitle a taxpayer to an extraordinary obsolescence or IRC § 165(a) retirement loss deduction on a specialized building when the taxpayer continues to use the facility (or any part of it) for laboratory operations, has not permanently withdrawn it from use, and management is still trying to find another use for it. Second, all research expenditures incurred under the Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF) federal contract prior to termination are disqualified from the IRC § 41 credit under the funded research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) because the government reimbursed VectraMat's incurred costs regardless of technical success and Termination for Convenience provisions insulated the contractor from financial loss (Fairchild Industries; Geosyntec). Third, by commingling government contract termination/closeout activities and internal commercial IR&D within Building 7's cost pool without strict project cost isolation, VectraMat exposes its post-termination IR&D claim to total disallowance for lack of substantiation under Coors Porcelain, 52 T.C. at 697–698.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Restructure Facility Governance and Execute Granular Asset Component Retirement

To avoid the Coors Porcelain blanket disallowance of the $9,200,000 building obsolescence claim, VectraMat must separate the multi-purpose building structure and active plasma-arc laboratory from the specialized, single-purpose missile tooling and CVI fixtures that genuinely became worthless upon contract cancellation. VectraMat must commission a detailed engineering cost segregation study partitioning Building 7's fixed-asset ledger into three distinct asset classes: the general structural shell and utility systems; the dual-use Plasma-Arc Wind Tunnel Laboratory bay; and the dedicated, missile-specific CVI mandrel reactors and toxic-gas scrubbers engineered exclusively for the cancelled federal missile geometry. Rather than claiming an abandonment or extraordinary obsolescence loss on Building 7 as a whole while continuing to operate its laboratory and market its floor space—the exact strategy rejected in Coors Porcelain—VectraMat must formally authorize via Board of Directors resolution the permanent retirement of the missile-specific CVI mandrel reactors, physically dismantle and sever them from utility connections, render them permanently unusable via documented third-party scrapping and demolition manifests, and write off only their segregated adjusted basis under IRC § 165(a) and Treas. Reg. § 1.167(a)-8(a)(3)–(4). For the remaining Building 7 structural shell and active plasma-arc laboratory bay, VectraMat must refrain from claiming an abandonment loss, maintain normal depreciation under IRC § 167 and § 168 (supported by an independent appraisal if adjusting remaining useful life where applicable), and classify the allocable depreciation of the active laboratory bay as an IRC § 174(c) research-use depreciation allowance under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(1).
Step 2: Establish a Strict Technical and Accounting Firewall Between Government SOW and IR&D

To protect the post-termination commercial orbital reentry tile research conducted inside Building 7's laboratory bay from being tainted by the cancelled government contract, VectraMat must establish an airtight accounting and technical firewall. Management must charter an independent project code (IR&D-2026-Orbital) backed by a formal internal R&D authorization memorandum proving that the commercial reusable thermal protection tile research falls entirely outside the scope of the terminated federal missile Statement of Work (SOW), receives zero direct federal reimbursement, and investigates distinct hypersonic oxidative-ablation uncertainties across multi-use orbital reentry cycles. Simultaneously, all administrative, legal, inventory-settlement, and demobilization labor associated with closing out the terminated federal contract must be isolated in a non-qualifying Contract Closeout cost center and strictly excluded from IRC § 174 and IRC § 41 claims, adhering to the IRS's position in FAA 20131102F (citing Coors Porcelain) that non-research administrative and termination expenditures lack the required nexus to experimental activities.
Step 3: Restructure Future Defense and Commercial R&D Contracts to Overcome the Funded Research Exclusion

For all prospective defense, aerospace, and commercial satellite development contracts utilizing Building 7, VectraMat's legal counsel must restructure contract terms prior to execution to satisfy both prongs of the funded research rules under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). First, to satisfy the Financial Risk Prong, VectraMat must transition away from Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee (CPFF) or unconditionally reimbursed time-and-materials contracts and execute Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) Milestone Deliverable Contracts tied to rigorous technical acceptance criteria. Under the restructured contract provisions, all progress or milestone payments must remain legally conditional and subject to refund or clawback until each prototype CMC propulsion component passes quantitative plasma-arc thermal shock acceptance testing, and VectraMat must bear full financial responsibility to re-engineer and cure any technical non-conformance at its own expense, aligning directly with Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995). Second, to satisfy the Substantial Rights Prong under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3), contract intellectual property clauses must explicitly preserve VectraMat's ownership of all background IP and vest in VectraMat either sole ownership or a perpetual, royalty-free, irrevocable license to use all foreground manufacturing processes, ceramic formulations, and experimental data across commercial and defense markets without paying royalties to the customer, satisfying the standards of Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), and Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Dkt. No. 405-17 (Dec. 6, 2019) (order granting summary judgment).
Step 4: Implement DCAA-Grade Experimentation Tracking and Substantiation

To ensure the post-termination IR&D-2026-Orbital project and future FFP milestones withstand IRS scrutiny, VectraMat must enforce a Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA)-compliant daily timekeeping system in which each of the 18 aerospace materials scientists records hours by specific Charge Number—strictly segregating funded CPFF closeout tasks from unfunded IR&D-2026-Orbital experimental tasks—and links every logged hour to a specific experimental test phase. Furthermore, every sacrificial CMC test coupon and plasma gas cylinder consumed in the Building 7 wind tunnel must be requisitioned via a digital bill of materials tied to a dated wind-tunnel test log documenting the exact temperature, enthalpy, and ablation failure metrics generated during the experiment. By integrating granular job-cost accounting ledgers with contemporaneous wind-tunnel test logs, executed FFP contracts, and third-party scrapping certificates for retired single-purpose fixtures, VectraMat constructs an authoritative evidentiary record that satisfies the burden of proof established in Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 52 T.C. at 688–698, aff'd, 429 F.2d 1 (10th Cir. 1970).

body.text: Conclusion and Strategic Synthesis for United States Tax Practitioners

Although Coors Porcelain Co. v. Commissioner, 52 T.C. 682 (1969), aff'd, 429 F.2d 1 (10th Cir. 1970), was decided under the 1954 Internal Revenue Code prior to the enactment of IRC § 41, its legal holdings remain deeply embedded in the structural architecture of United States R&D tax law. Because IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) expressly conditions eligibility for the federal research tax credit upon establishing that expenditures connected with the research may be treated as expenses under IRC § 174, the IRS and federal courts continuously invoke Coors Porcelain as a primary gatekeeping authority.

For corporate tax executives, R&D tax attorneys, and technical advisors practicing in the United States, Coors Porcelain establishes four enduring compliance mandates. First, alterations that do not restore manufacturing machinery to a sound state but improve it to function in a different manner are permanent improvements or betterments that must be capitalized under IRC § 263(a), and the costs of component material, labor, construction, and installation are excluded from experimental expenditures by Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4), unless the taxpayer can prove through rigorous, contemporaneous technical documentation that specific costs were incurred for expendable pilot models or preliminary experimental engineering aimed at resolving genuine technological uncertainty in the experimental or laboratory sense. Second, commingling experimental design and testing costs with capital equipment retooling inside an unsegregated work order is fatal; without contemporaneous cost bifurcation under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3)–(4), the court will find it impossible to segregate any allocable R&D portion and will require the entire expenditure to be charged to capital account. Third, substantive technical eligibility must be paired with strict procedural compliance under IRC § 174, IRC § 174A, and IRC § 446(e) to ensure that the taxpayer's R&D accounting method has been validly adopted and maintained. Fourth, when specialized government or commercial R&D contracts are cancelled, taxpayers cannot claim extraordinary obsolescence or abandonment losses on dual-use facilities that continue to house laboratory operations or await commercial redeployment, nor can they claim IRC § 41 credits without structuring contracts to bear financial risk, retain substantial IP rights, and strictly segregate funded contract deliverables from independent R&D.
